title: Senior's toolkit: measuring, not guessing
summary: Big-O tells you how code scales; Stopwatch and BenchmarkDotNet tell you what it really costs. Use both.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: measuring, not guessing
steps.body: In a performance review, "I think this is faster" loses to a number. Experienced .NET engineers know the complexity of the calls they make, and measure with the right tool before and after a change.

toolkit.what: The costs to know by heart, because they decide whether code survives 100,000 items.
flags: O(1) amortised (the array doubles when full)
O(n log n); `Array.BinarySearch` on sorted data is O(log n)
toolkit.example:
var seen = new HashSet<int>(ids);   // O(n) once
if (seen.Contains(id)) ...          // then O(1) per lookup

toolkit.what: A high-resolution timer for a quick, rough measurement. Warm up first (the first call includes JIT compilation) and time many iterations, not one.
flags: the same without allocating a Stopwatch (.NET 7+)

toolkit.what: Measure only optimised code. A Debug build turns off JIT optimisations and can be several times slower, which makes timings meaningless.
flags: run the benchmark project from the repo root

toolkit.what: BenchmarkDotNet, the standard .NET benchmarking library (`dotnet add package BenchmarkDotNet`). It warms up, runs many iterations and reports statistics, so the numbers are trustworthy.
flags: the method others are compared against (Ratio column)
run every benchmark for each size, to see the growth
add the Allocated and Gen0 columns
run only matching benchmarks; needs `args` passed in, e.g. `BenchmarkSwitcher.FromAssembly(typeof(Program).Assembly).Run(args)`

toolkit.what: How to read BenchmarkDotNet's table: compare Mean and Ratio across sizes to see the real growth, and Allocated to see GC pressure.
flags: noise; if they are large, the result is not stable
toolkit.example:
| Method       | N      | Mean        | Ratio | Allocated |
| ListContains | 100000 | 21,410.0 ns |  1.00 |         - |
| SetContains  | 100000 |      4.1 ns |  0.00 |         - |

toolkit.what: A quick check of how much a piece of code allocates, without a profiler.
flags: how many gen-0 collections have run

steps.prompt: Match each call to its cost.
An import endpoint is fine in tests (100 rows) and times out in production (100,000 rows). The profiler points here. What is the fix?
options: Build `var known = new HashSet<string>(existing);` once and call `known.Contains`: O(n + m) instead of O(n × m)
Sort `existing` before the loop and keep `Contains`
steps.explain: `List.Contains` scans the list, so the loop is O(n × m): 10¹⁰ comparisons at that size. Sorting does not help `Contains`, which still scans. Parallelism divides by the core count at best; the hash set removes the scan.

steps.prompt: Count the steps. What does this print?
steps.explain: Every pair once: 7 + 6 + ... + 1 + 0 = 8 × 7 / 2 = 28. Comparing all pairs is n(n-1)/2, still O(n²): double n and the work roughly quadruples.

steps.prompt: Complete the benchmark so it reports allocations and runs for two input sizes.
steps.explain: `[Fact]`, `[Theory]` and `[InlineData]` are xUnit test attributes. A benchmark is not a test: run it with `dotnet run -c Release`, never `dotnet test`.

steps.prompt: A teammate times a method once with `Stopwatch` in a Debug build and reports "it takes 40 ms". What are the two biggest problems?
options: One call includes JIT compilation, and Debug code is unoptimised: warm up, repeat many times, use Release (or BenchmarkDotNet)
`Stopwatch` is accurate only to one second
Stopwatch measures CPU time, not wall-clock time
Nothing; one measurement in Debug is representative
steps.explain: `Stopwatch` has sub-microsecond resolution and measures wall-clock time. The trap is the first call (JIT) and the Debug build. BenchmarkDotNet handles both, and warns you if the build is not optimised.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Before you optimise, write down the Big-O of the hot loop and measure it at the real input size, in Release. Back every performance claim in a pull request with a BenchmarkDotNet table, before and after.
